narrative:
The 2023 Pittsburgh Pirates arrived with genuine optimism, and for one glorious month they looked like believers were right. A 19-9 April put them among the best records in baseball, built on timely hitting and a bullpen that was mostly holding together. The young core — Ke'Bryan Hayes, Bryan Reynolds, a rotation of promising arms — seemed ready to take the next step, and PNC Park buzzed with a energy that hadn't been felt in years.

Then May arrived like a cold front off the Ohio River. An 8-18 collapse erased the goodwill almost overnight, and the bullpen that had carried April began to crack. Robert Stephenson surrendered a crushing three-run homer to Eugenio Suarez in late May that captured the misery perfectly — leads evaporating, close games slipping away. June and July were more of the same, a grinding 19-31 stretch where the Pirates couldn't buy a save and closer David Bednar was repeatedly put in impossible situations. Moments of genuine joy — Carlos Santana's walk-off blast on June 30, Jason Delay's clutch double days earlier, Jared Triolo's Independence Day single — were isolated islands of hope in a sea of losing.

August offered a minor reprieve, a nearly .500 month where the young roster showed flashes of what it might become. Triolo's first career home run, a three-run shot that lifted the club, and Hayes's late-August blast suggested the roster's ceiling was still worth believing in. September became a mixed bag of promise and frustration — Joshua Palacios going deep with Andrew McCutchen, the living link to better Pirates days, before the bullpen again let games bleed away to the Braves and Yankees down the stretch.

The final ledger read 76-86, a painful fall from April's heights. The Pirates scored nearly 100 fewer runs than they allowed, and their 4.60 ERA told the real story: a young team with offensive promise but a pitching staff — particularly in relief — that simply couldn't hold the line when it mattered most. The foundation is intriguing, but 2023 proved that promise and production are two very different things.

chapters.title: April's Believers
chapters.description: A blazing 19-9 April announces the Pirates as a legitimate contender, even as early bullpen cracks hint at trouble ahead.

chapters.title: May Collapse
chapters.description: An 8-18 May unravels all of April's goodwill as the bullpen implodes and leads evaporate night after night.

chapters.title: Sinking Through Summer
chapters.description: June and July produce a brutal 19-31 stretch, though clutch moments from Santana, Delay, and Triolo provide rare oxygen.

chapters.title: Fighting Back to .500
chapters.description: A nearly even August sees the young Pirates flash their ceiling, with Triolo and Hayes delivering timely power.

chapters.title: Too Little, Too Late
chapters.description: September brings flickers of hope including a Palacios blast alongside McCutchen, but the bullpen keeps surrendering games as playoff dreams fade for good.
